changes.before: If take(3) becomes take(1), what is realized?
changes.after: A lazy sequence waits to do work until something asks for its items.

before:
Calling each without a block returns an Enumerator. lazy builds a demand-driven pipeline rather than eagerly computing a full intermediate collection; force materializes the requested lazy results.

The no-block each call takes no explicit argument here and returns an Enumerator rather than executing an iteration block. class reports the kind of the returned object.
```ruby
stream = [1, 2].each
puts stream.class
```
It prints:
```text
Enumerator
```

The endless range 1.. can keep producing values. take(3) limits demand before force, so this pipeline terminates. Do not force an unbounded stream or assume laziness makes an expensive individual element cheap.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
numbers = (1..).lazy.map { |n| n * 2 }.take(3)
p numbers.force

```
Expected output or behavior: [2, 4, 6]. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Explain why moving force before take is unsafe for an endless range. You may trace it without a Ruby interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A lazy sequence waits to do work until something asks for its items.
Although the input range has no end, only its first three doubled numbers are wanted.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```ruby
numbers = (1..).lazy.map { |n| n * 2 }.take(3)
p numbers.force
```
The output is `[2, 4, 6]`. Force asks for those numbers, so the program finishes after three items.
Reduce the limit to one and follow the first input.
